title: Evidence-Aware Missense Variant Interpretation with a Typed-Decision Language Model
content: The interpretation of missense variants requires the integration of sequence, structural and evolutionary evidence, yet most computational predictors operate on specialised representations rather than curator-readable descriptions. We investigate whether a typed-decision language model can use this evidence directly. Using GLiDE-9B, we construct four increasingly informative text representations and evaluate them on a gene-disjoint ClinVar benchmark derived from 199,243 germline missense variants. On 33,478 commonly scored test variants, zero-shot ROC-AUC rises from 0.817 with variant-level information alone to 0.933 with conservation. Low-rank adaptation on 20,000 gene-disjoint ClinVar training variants yields ROC-AUC 0.976 and average precision 0.944, compared with 0.973 and 0.941 for REVEL; the difference in ROC-AUC is significant (DeLong p = 4.5 × 10−5), whereas the average-precision difference is not (p = 0.14). A second adapter trained using population- and primate-derived proxy labels, without ClinVar labels as optimisation targets, achieves ROC-AUC 0.940 and average precision 0.862; however, ClinVar validation labels are still used for checkpoint selection and calibration. The ClinVar- trained model achieves a calibrated Brier score of 0.054 and validation-derived thresholds corresponding to PP3/BP4 evidence strengths up to Strong. These results are qualified by lower performance than leading comparators when ranking variants within individual genes, more modest associations with functional assays, and near-chance performance in autism and congenital heart disease case–control comparisons. The findings support evidence-aware decision modelling as a complementary approach to missense variant prioritisation, while emphasising the need for prospective, independently curated validation before clinical use
